extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars in philosophy/literature (Faculty of Philosophy and Letters)
extracted.subtask_description: An academic lecture presenting criteria for what counts as 'Letters' (literature), how literature differs from Science, and how to judge style, translation, originality, and workmanship in literary composition. Intended to guide students in evaluating and producing literary works and in forming critical taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature implies writing (permanent record) and addresses the ear
rubrics_metrics.description: Literature, from the derivation of the word, implies writing — the permanent record of speech — and in its primary idea it addresses the ear, not the eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lecturer notes that even when written, literature retains characteristics of speech (we use terms like 'saying', 'speaking', 'telling'), so judges should attend to its oral qualities (phrase, diction, rhythm) rather than treating it merely as printed information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature is the personal use of language (subjective expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Literature is the personal use or exercise of language: it expresses subjective thoughts and feelings peculiar to the individual author, not objective scientific truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because literature proceeds from one individual's voice and inward world, critical assessment should look for distinct personality, original viewpoints, and the faithful expression of the author's mind; it is not merely an account of 'things' but a manifestation of 'thoughts'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Literature from Science (words as expression vs symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science uses words as symbols for universal, objective truths; literature uses language in its full compass — phraseology, idiom, style, composition, rhythm, eloquence — to embody thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works resembling encyclopedic or symbolic treatment (Euclid, scientific treatises) belong to Science rather than Literature for critical purposes. Evaluators should not conflate technical clarity with literary merit; different standards apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style should be authentic and reflect the author's mind (not bought or manufactured)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style is an image of the author's mind and person; genuine style cannot be merely purchased or manufactured by a hired writer without loss of authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lecture condemns the practice of authors who 'buy' a style for their matter (examples: hiring a writer to gild lectures). Assessors should penalize inauthentic, outsourced diction and value unity of thought and expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elaborateness is not necessarily affectation — craftsmanship and revision are legitimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Elaborate composition and careful workmanship (revision, multiple drafts) can be the appropriate and necessary means by which genius brings its conceptions into fitting language; elaborate style is not ipso facto mere conceit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Virgil, Gibbon, Demosthenes, Addison) show that great writers often labour and revise. Rubrics should allow for careful craftsmanship, distinguishing between thought-serving elaboration and mere verbal trickery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and majesty can coexist; simplicity is not the sole mark of excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Sacred Scripture combines simplicity with majesty, but classical literature can also be simple and majestic; the presence of ornament does not automatically disqualify a work from being great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should avoid reducing excellence to 'simplicity' alone; instead judge whether simplicity or ornament suits the subject and arises from powerful thought rather than from affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease of translation is not a valid test of literary excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: To be capable of easy translation is no test of the excellence of a composition; the assumption that languages are equivalent in expressive resources is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lecturer argues against the idea that works which 'bear translating' are superior (example: claim that Scripture translates easily whereas classics do not). Evaluators should not downgrade works because they lose certain formal effects in translation; instead assess authorial mastery in the original idiom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style must be appropriate to subject, speaker, and occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: The propriety of diction and degree of ornament should match the subject-matter and the author's role — e.g., Cicero's majestic flow suits a Roman statesman; a gentlemanly neatness suits other writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rubrics should include suitability: whether language and tone are in keeping with the speaker/author's purpose and the demands of the subject, rather than judging all styles by a single narrow aesthetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary power is manifest in expansion and expressive form as much as in condensed statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Great authors may expand simple ideas into rich periods and rhythms (Shakespeare, Cicero), and such expansion can be the contemporaneous offspring of emotion or imagination rather than gratuitous verbosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should recognize legitimate rhetorical expansion and rhythmic/periodic complexity as expressive of intellectual power, not merely as 'verbiage'; distinguish energetic fulness from pointless diffuseness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual authorship and unity of voice are essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Because literature proceeds from an individual, two persons cannot properly be the authors of the same speech or write the same lecture; style and thought belong to a single mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should favor works with a coherent, unified authorial voice and be wary of collaborative or composite texts that lack personal presence or singular perspective.
